title: Krishna vanishes from the dance
hookLine: on autumn's moonlit nights the gopis dance with Krishna, grow proud, and he's gone: the Hindu teaching on the ego
carry: ahankara: pride hides god, longing brings him back

lines: RICE AND MILK UNDER THE MOON.
cards: Autumn, in Charaka's year, is a jolt: the clouds clear, the sun comes out hard after the rains, and his advice turns to cooling food and moonlight early in the night.
Hindus give autumn its own full moon, Sharad Purnima, and in some homes a bowl of rice and milk is left out under it overnight. The Bhagavata Purana sets its most well-known night in this season too.
Autumn nights, jasmine in bloom, the moon coming up. And from the forest, a flute.

teach.b: When the gopis, the cowherd women of Vraja, hear Krishna's flute, they drop everything. One leaves milk on the fire. One leaves her meal half eaten.

They run to the forest, and Krishna plays and dances with them by the Yamuna in the moonlight. Then, the Bhagavata says, the gopis begin to feel proud. Each thinks, of all the women in the world, I'm the one he chose.
And Krishna disappears. Just like that, the circle is empty. The gopis search the forest, asking the trees and vines if they've seen him.

They act out his childhood to feel near him. At last they sit by the river and sing, simply longing for him, and Krishna returns and stands among them. Only then does the great circle dance begin: the raas.
The text says plainly why he left: to take away their pride. That's the teaching: ahankara, the ego, literally the I-maker.
In Hindu thought it's the sense of me and mine that stands between us and God, and Krishna's vanishing shows it can creep in even through love. The gopis didn't lose him by loving too much.
They lost him when the love turned into, look at me. He came back when it turned into longing again.

teach.h: HE VANISHES; THEY LONG FOR HIM
teach.b: That's why bhakti teachers hold up the gopis as the great devotees: not because they never got proud, but because they never stopped longing.
Many Hindus remember the raas on Sharad Purnima, and the circle dances of the autumn festivals share its name.

how: On Sharad Purnima, autumn's full moon, many Hindus remember Krishna's raas with the gopis, and some families leave rice cooked in milk under the moon overnight; people who follow Ayurveda cool the body in autumn with sweet and bitter foods, ghee and early-night moonlight.

games.q: in the moonlit forest with Krishna, each gopi thinks: of everyone, he chose me. what happens next?
o: Krishna disappears, to take away their pride.
games.why: ahankara, the ego, hides God. when the gopis stop showing off and simply long for him, singing by the river, he comes back.

practice: Sit, and let the breath be cool and easy, like an autumn evening. Notice the little voice that narrates you: how am I doing, am I good at this. Don't fight it.
Just see it, and each time, come back to the breath. If you pray, sing or say one name of Krishna, the way the gopis sang by the river. If you don't, sit in plain thanks for the turning year.

wordCard.voice: The seasons. In autumn, Charaka's moonlight cools a sudden sun, and the Bhagavata's moonlit raas shows Krishna leaving when pride comes in, and returning to longing. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ahankara, the I-maker. In Hindu thought, the sense of me and mine that stands between us and God.

carryVoice: Your line: ahankara, pride hides God, and longing brings him back. Dance your best, for him. Rest well.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.29–33 (autumn nights; the flute; the gopis leave their work; their play in the moonlit forest; the gopis' pride and Krishna's disappearance to remove it, 10.29.47–48; the search; the Gopi Gita, 10.31; his return, 10.32; the raas, the great circle dance, 10.33)
